title: Rollout error growth with horizon: how fast does error accumulate in autoregressive use?
summary: When a model is applied to its own output step after step, small errors feed on themselves. This plot shows the error against the number of steps (the horizon) on a log axis, with an exponential reference line for the growth rate.

media.alt: Semi-log plot of relative error against rollout step from 0 to 100: three model curves rise roughly exponentially, with an amber dotted exponential reference; the third model reaches the dashed line marked error equals signal scale near step 76 and saturates at about 2; the regularised model ends at about 3e-2.
media.caption: Reference render of class F6.9 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: How fast does error accumulate in autoregressive use?
read_the_figure.axes: x: rollout step n (0 to 100). y: relative error, logarithmic (1e-5 to 10). A dashed horizontal line marks relative error 1 (error equal to the signal scale).
look_at: Is each curve a straight line on this log axis (exponential growth)? What is its slope?
At what step does each curve reach the line error = signal scale?
Do the curves cross, so that the best model at step 0 is not the best at step 100?
Is the exponential reference labelled with its rate?
as_drawn: Three models and the reference e^(0.09 n): model A (teal) hugs the reference from 1e-4 at step 0 to about 0.8 at step 100.

Model B, regularised (blue dashed), starts higher (2e-4) but grows more slowly, ending near 3e-2. Model C (rose) starts lowest (5e-5), grows fastest, crosses error = 1 near step 76 and saturates at about 2.
The three curves all pass through about 6e-4 near step 20, so the ranking at step 0 (C best, B worst) is reversed by step 40.
The dashed line at error = 1 is labelled error = signal scale; the amber dotted reference is labelled with its rate 0.09.
read_the_figure.proves: The slope of the straight part of each curve on this axis is the growth rate of the rollout error, and the intercept with the line error = 1 is the usable horizon. It does not say why the error grows, which can come from the model, the data or the intrinsic sensitivity of the system.
if_wrong: Curves that bend downwards: growth slower than exponential (algebraic), or error saturating.
Saturation at a constant level: the model has lost all information (prediction is as good as a random state).
No exponential reference: the reader cannot judge the rate by eye.
must_check: log axis: exponential growth is a straight line on a log axis, and only there can the rate be read.
exponential reference: it fixes a rate to compare against, which the eye cannot do for a curve by itself.

terms.meaning: Applying a one-step model repeatedly to its own output.
The number of steps over which a rollout stays useful.
The exponent lambda in e_n = e_0 exp(lambda n); on a semi-log plot it is the slope.
The number of steps for the error to double: ln 2 / lambda.
Error divided by the size of the signal; one means the prediction is as far off as the signal is large.
The average exponential rate at which nearby trajectories of the true system separate; it limits how well any model can forecast.

remember: e_n = e_0 exp(lambda n) is a straight line of slope lambda on a log axis.
Usable horizon n* = ln(1 / e_0) / lambda.
A better start does not guarantee a better horizon.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position on x is the number of steps and position on y is the relative error on a log scale. Each model has its own colour, line style and marker. The amber dotted line is a theoretical exponential, the grey dashed line marks the scale at which the error equals the signal. Markers appear only every few steps so they do not hide the lines.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: errors in a rollout are fed back in, so each step starts from a slightly wrong place. If the model amplifies that error by a constant factor each step, the error grows exponentially. On a log axis exponential growth is a straight line, so a glance tells you the rate, and the point where the line meets the signal-scale line is how far ahead the model can be trusted.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: The early part, where all curves are near each other, says little about the late behaviour: here the best model at step 0 is the worst at step 100. Averaging over initial conditions on a log axis can hide a few trajectories that blow up. If the true system is chaotic, even a perfect model cannot beat the system's own sensitivity: the growth rate cannot go below the Lyapunov exponent in units of steps. And the saturation at error of about 2 is not a property of the model, only of the clipping of the data.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: Plot the median and the 10 to 90 percent interval over many initial states. Compare with the growth of an error in the initial condition of the true system (the intrinsic limit). Report the horizon at which the error reaches a fixed fraction of the signal as a single number per model.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add a band of the 10th to 90th percentile over 200 starts for each model, a vertical tick at each model's usable horizon, and a grey line for the growth of an initial perturbation in the true system.

steps.title: Exponential growth is a straight line
steps.note: The slope on a log axis is lambda (per step); replace ln by log10 and the numbers change by a constant.

steps.title: The rate from two points
steps.note: Model A: from 1e-4 at n = 0 to 0.8 at n = 100 gives lambda = ln(8000) / 100 = 0.090, doubling every 7.7 steps.

steps.title: The usable horizon
steps.note: A: 102 steps, B: 170 steps (from 2e-4, rate 0.05), C: 76 steps (from 5e-5, rate 0.13). The ranking by start error is the reverse of the ranking by horizon.

worked.title: Reading the rollout error in the reference render
worked.problem: (1) What growth rate has model A and how long does it take its error to double? (2) At what step does model C reach error = 1 and why does it flatten afterwards? (3) Which model has the longest usable horizon and what is it?

solution.text: (1) Model A runs from 1e-4 at n = 0 to about 0.8 at n = 100.
(2) Model C starts at 5e-5 and grows at 0.13 per step.
It flattens near 2 because the plotted error is capped (a saturated prediction is as wrong as an unrelated state); the cap is a property of the data, not of the model.
(3) Model B has the smallest rate (0.05) and so the longest horizon.

worked.answer: A: rate 0.09, doubling every 7.7 steps; C reaches error 1 at step 76 and saturates; B, the regularised model, has the longest horizon at about 170 steps, despite starting with the largest error.

analyze.q: Why does regularisation help the long horizon even though the starting error is larger?
What is the relationship between a model's growth rate and the Lyapunov exponent of the true chaotic system?
analyze.hint: Even a perfect model with a tiny initial error diverges at the system's own rate.

analyze.q: What would you plot to see how much of model A's growth is intrinsic to the system?
analyze.hint: Perturb the true system's initial condition by the same amount.

evaluate.q: A paper reports only the error at step 1. How much does that tell you about the usable horizon?

create: Redraw with the 10 to 90 percent band over many starts and a tick at each model's horizon.
Add the growth of a tiny perturbation in the true system as a grey reference line and compare rates.

checks.q: Why is exponential growth a straight line on this plot?
checks.answer: ln e_n = ln e_0 + lambda n is linear in n, so on a log axis the curve is a straight line with slope lambda.

checks.q: An error is 1e-3 at step 10 and 1e-2 at step 30. What is the growth rate and the doubling time?
Model C has the smallest error at step 1 but the shortest horizon. Explain.
checks.answer: Its error grows faster (a larger rate), so a small starting point is overtaken: the horizon depends mainly on the growth rate, with only a logarithmic dependence on the starting error.
